A17U.what: Owns business parks, logistics facilities and data centres in Singapore, Australia, the US and Europe, and leases them to corporate tenants.
A17U.rev: Singapore is roughly 60-65% of asset value, with the US, Australia and Europe the rest. Business parks and industrial are the largest categories, data centres the highest-value.
A17U.gm: REIT metrics: net property income margin around 70%, gearing in the high 30s, weighted average lease expiry around 3-4 years, positive rental reversions.
A17U.mgmt: Managed by CapitaLand Investment as sponsor. The sponsor pipeline is a genuine advantage for acquisitions.
A17U.comp: Mapletree Industrial Trust, ESR-REIT, Frasers Logistics in the same tenant pool.
A17U.moat: Scale in Singapore business park space - a category with limited land supply - plus tenant relationships with multinationals.
A17U.ind: Logistics and data centre demand is strong; business park demand depends on office-style occupancy which has been mixed.
A17U.risk: Refinancing at higher rates while business park occupancy softens - the double squeeze on distributions.
A17U.implied: A yield above 5% implies stable occupancy and modest rental growth with no distribution cut.
A17U.debate: Bulls like the diversified industrial exposure and sponsor pipeline. Bears note business parks face the same hybrid-work question as offices.
A17U.disprove: Portfolio occupancy falling below 92%; rental reversions turning negative; gearing above 40%; distribution per unit declining.

Y92.what: Brews and distributes beer and spirits in Thailand and Vietnam - Chang beer, Thai whisky brands and a stake in Sabeco.
Y92.rev: Spirits (Thai white and brown spirits) is the profit engine, beer the largest revenue line, plus non-alcoholic beverages and food. Thailand and Vietnam dominate.
Y92.gm: Gross margin in the 20s-30s. Thai spirits are highly profitable with entrenched distribution; beer is more competitive and excise-heavy.
Y92.mgmt: Controlled by the Sirivadhanabhakdi family through TCC. Singapore-listed but a Thai company, with a long-delayed plan to list the beer business separately.
Y92.comp: Boon Rawd (Singha) and Carlsberg in Thai beer, Heineken and Habeco in Vietnam.
Y92.moat: Dominant share of Thai spirits with a distribution network reaching hundreds of thousands of outlets, plus licences that are effectively unobtainable for newcomers.
Y92.ind: Thai consumption has been weak with high household debt; Vietnamese beer volumes hit by drink-driving enforcement.
Y92.risk: Thai excise tax changes, or Vietnamese consumption staying depressed so the expensive Sabeco stake keeps underperforming.
Y92.implied: A low P/E and high dividend yield imply little growth is expected - the market has priced in the Thai consumer malaise.
Y92.debate: Bulls say a dominant spirits franchise at a single-digit multiple with a possible beer listing catalyst. Bears note the Sabeco acquisition was expensive and Thai demand is weak.
Y92.disprove: Thai spirits volumes declining; Sabeco profit contribution falling; net debt to EBITDA not improving; the beer listing shelved again.

C07.what: Distributes and retails motor vehicles in Singapore (Mercedes, Mitsubishi, Kia) and holds a controlling stake in Astra International of Indonesia.
C07.rev: Astra Indonesia is the overwhelming majority of earnings - cars, motorcycles, heavy equipment, mining, financial services. Singapore motor operations are a small part.
C07.gm: Look through to Astra: Indonesian car and motorcycle market share, heavy equipment (Komatsu) sales and coal mining contribution.
C07.mgmt: Part of the Jardine Matheson group, which controls it. Effectively a listed vehicle for Astra exposure.
C07.comp: In Indonesia, Chinese EV brands attacking Astra's Toyota and Daihatsu share; in Singapore, other authorised dealers.
C07.moat: Astra's dealer and financing network across Indonesia is decades deep and hard to replicate - but market share in cars is being eroded.
C07.ind: Indonesian vehicle sales have been soft; coal and heavy equipment cyclical.
C07.risk: Chinese EV brands taking Indonesian market share from Astra faster than expected.
C07.implied: A single-digit P/E with a high dividend yield implies the market expects Astra's earnings to decline.
C07.debate: Bulls say cheap access to Indonesian consumption with a strong dividend. Bears see structural share loss in the core car business.
C07.disprove: Astra car market share falling below 50%; Indonesian vehicle sales declining; coal contribution shrinking; dividend cut.

U96.what: Generates and sells electricity and provides urban utilities - gas, water, waste - in Singapore, India, the UK and Southeast Asia, with a growing renewables portfolio.
U96.rev: Gas and related services (Singapore power generation) is the profit core; renewables (solar and wind in India and China) is the growth engine; integrated urban solutions the rest.
U96.gm: Watch the spark spread in Singapore power generation, renewables capacity added, and net gearing - this is a capital-intensive utility.
U96.mgmt: Wong Kim Yin is CEO. Temasek holds roughly 49% - the Sembcorp Marine separation left a cleaner energy company.
U96.comp: Keppel Infrastructure and YTL PowerSeraya in Singapore generation, regional independent power producers in renewables.
U96.moat: Singapore generation licences and long-term power purchase agreements, plus a first-mover renewables position in India.
U96.ind: Asian electricity demand is growing; the energy transition is creating a large renewables build-out.
U96.risk: Singapore spark spreads normalising downward as new capacity arrives, while renewables returns are lower than the gas business they replace.
U96.implied: A low-teens P/E implies the renewables build-out replaces gas earnings without a return-on-capital decline.
U96.debate: Bulls say a transition story with strong cash flows funding renewables growth. Bears note Singapore generation margins are at cyclical highs and renewables earn less.
U96.disprove: Singapore spark spreads compressing; renewables capacity additions below target; net gearing rising; return on equity declining.

G13.what: Operates Resorts World Sentosa - the casino, Universal Studios theme park and hotels - under a Singapore duopoly licence.
G13.rev: Gaming is roughly 60-65% of revenue, non-gaming (theme park, hotels, attractions) the rest. Singapore is essentially the whole business.
G13.gm: EBITDA margin in the 30s-40s. Casino economics are excellent once the property is built; the current expansion is a large capital commitment.
G13.mgmt: Part of the Genting group, which holds roughly 53%. Tan Sri Lim Kok Thay controls the parent.
G13.comp: Marina Bay Sands is the only other Singapore licence holder; regionally, Macau, Manila and Korean casinos compete for tourists.
G13.moat: A government-granted duopoly with the casino licence extended to 2030s, plus Universal Studios which no competitor can replicate.
G13.ind: Regional tourism to Singapore is recovering; Chinese outbound travel remains below pre-pandemic levels.
G13.risk: The multi-billion RWS expansion delivering lower returns than expected, or Chinese high-roller demand not returning.
G13.implied: The valuation with a large net cash balance implies modest growth and continued high dividends.
G13.debate: Bulls say a licensed duopoly with net cash, a high dividend and an expansion pipeline. Bears note VIP gaming volatility and a heavy capex cycle depressing free cash flow.
G13.disprove: Gaming volumes declining; expansion capex exceeding budget; hold rates masking weak underlying volume; Chinese visitor arrivals not recovering.

U14.what: Develops and invests in property in Singapore and internationally, and owns hotels through Pan Pacific - a family-controlled property group.
U14.rev: Property investment (rental from Singapore offices and malls), property development, and hotel operations across Asia Pacific.
U14.gm: Look at recurring rental income coverage of interest, net asset value per share, and the discount the share price trades at to that value.
U14.mgmt: The Wee family (also behind UOB) controls it; Wee Ee Lim is CEO. Family control means a long horizon and a persistent valuation discount.
U14.comp: City Developments, GuocoLand, Frasers Property and CapitaLand in Singapore development and investment.
U14.moat: Prime Singapore commercial assets and a conservative balance sheet - not a competitive moat so much as asset quality.
U14.ind: Singapore office and retail rents are stable; residential is constrained by cooling measures.
U14.risk: Singapore property cooling measures tightening further, or higher interest costs on development financing.
U14.implied: A large discount to net asset value implies the market does not expect the assets to be monetised.
U14.debate: Bulls say you buy prime Singapore property at a steep discount with a safe balance sheet. Bears say family-controlled property companies trade at discounts forever.
U14.disprove: Net asset value per share declining; rental income falling; development margins compressing; the discount widening rather than narrowing.

C09.what: Develops residential and commercial property in Singapore and internationally, and owns hotels through Millennium and Copthorne.
C09.rev: Property development (Singapore residential) is the largest earnings driver, hotel operations the largest revenue line, plus rental income from investment properties.
C09.gm: Development margins have compressed as land costs rose; hotel RevPAR has recovered. Net gearing is high relative to Singapore peers.
C09.mgmt: The Kwek family controls it through Hong Leong; the 2024 boardroom dispute between father and son raised genuine governance concerns.
C09.comp: UOL, GuocoLand, Frasers Property and CapitaLand in Singapore residential.
C09.moat: A large Singapore land bank and a global hotel portfolio - asset-heavy, but not a competitive moat.
C09.ind: Singapore residential sales volumes are constrained by cooling measures; hotels have recovered.
C09.risk: High gearing combined with slow inventory sell-down and any further governance disruption.
C09.implied: A very large discount to net asset value implies the market doubts both the asset values and the governance.
C09.debate: Bulls say deeply discounted assets with a potential unlocking through divestments. Bears point at gearing, a China project write-down history and the public boardroom fight.
C09.disprove: Net gearing rising above 100%; unsold inventory ageing; further impairments; governance disputes resurfacing.

5E2.what: Builds and repairs offshore rigs, floating production vessels and now offshore wind installation vessels - the merged Sembcorp Marine and Keppel Offshore and Marine.
5E2.rev: Newbuild projects (FPSOs, wind vessels) plus repairs and upgrades. Order book is concentrated in a handful of very large projects.
5E2.gm: Margins have been thin to negative because of legacy contracts; the question is whether newer contracts are priced profitably.
5E2.mgmt: Chris Ong Leng Yeow leads the company after a period of instability. Temasek is the largest shareholder. It has been through corruption-related provisions tied to legacy Keppel Offshore and Marine projects.
5E2.comp: Korean yards (Hyundai, Samsung), Chinese yards, and Sembcorp's own past self - global yard capacity is ample.
5E2.moat: Scale of Singapore yard facilities and FPSO integration capability, but this is a project business with limited pricing power.
5E2.ind: Offshore oil capex has recovered and offshore wind installation demand is growing - the cycle has turned up.
5E2.risk: Another loss-making project or legacy provision, which has been the pattern rather than the exception.
5E2.implied: The price implies the order book converts at positive margins - which the company has repeatedly failed to deliver historically.
5E2.debate: Bulls say a record order book, a cleaner balance sheet and an offshore upcycle. Bears point at a long history of cost overruns, provisions and dilution.
5E2.disprove: New project charges; order book margin guidance cut; net cash position deteriorating; further legacy legal provisions.

EB5.what: Grows oil palm and produces crude palm oil in Indonesia, with a young and productive plantation base.
EB5.rev: Crude palm oil and palm kernel sales, mostly within Indonesia and to export markets. A pure upstream plantation play.
EB5.gm: Margins track the palm oil price against cash cost per tonne. First Resources has among the lowest costs and youngest tree profiles in the sector.
EB5.mgmt: The Fangiono family controls the company - founder-led with substantial insider ownership.
EB5.comp: Golden Agri-Resources, Bumitama Agri, Wilmar upstream, Malaysian planters.
EB5.moat: Low cost per tonne and a favourable tree age profile. In a commodity, being the low-cost producer is the only durable advantage.
EB5.ind: Palm oil prices have been firm on tight supply and biodiesel mandates in Indonesia.
EB5.risk: Indonesian export levies and biodiesel policy changes, or a palm price fall combined with rising fertiliser costs.
EB5.implied: A low P/E implies the market expects palm prices to mean-revert lower.
EB5.debate: Bulls like the low cost base, net cash and high dividend at a single-digit multiple. Bears say commodity producers deserve low multiples at cycle peaks.
EB5.disprove: Crude palm oil prices falling below cash costs; yields declining; Indonesian export levy increases; replanting capex rising.

N2IU.what: Owns VivoCity and Mapletree Business City in Singapore plus office and retail assets in Hong Kong, China, Japan and Korea.
N2IU.rev: Singapore is roughly 60% of net property income (VivoCity is the single largest asset), Hong Kong ~20% and the problem child, China, Japan and Korea the rest.
N2IU.gm: REIT metrics: net property income margin around 75%, gearing around 38-40%, and the Festival Walk Hong Kong valuation is the key swing factor.
N2IU.mgmt: Managed by Mapletree Investments, a Temasek subsidiary and the sponsor.
N2IU.comp: CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust and Frasers Centrepoint in Singapore retail; Link REIT in Hong Kong.
N2IU.moat: VivoCity is Singapore's largest mall with a captive catchment - a genuinely strong asset. The overseas portfolio is more ordinary.
N2IU.ind: Singapore retail is strong; Hong Kong retail rents have fallen sharply as shoppers cross into Shenzhen.
N2IU.risk: Festival Walk in Hong Kong requiring further valuation write-downs and negative rental reversions.
N2IU.implied: A high distribution yield implies the market expects further Hong Kong weakness and possible distribution pressure.
N2IU.debate: Bulls say you get VivoCity cheaply because of Hong Kong. Bears say the Hong Kong and China exposure keeps the discount justified.
N2IU.disprove: Festival Walk reversions staying deeply negative; China occupancy falling; gearing rising above 41%; distribution per unit declining again.

D01.what: Runs pan-Asian retail - Guardian and Mannings health and beauty, 7-Eleven convenience, supermarkets, IKEA franchises and a stake in Yonghui in China.
D01.rev: Health and beauty is the profit engine, convenience stores the largest store count, food retail the largest revenue but weakest margin. Hong Kong, Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and mainland China.
D01.gm: Health and beauty carries the highest margin; food retail is thin. The turnaround has been about exiting low-return formats.
D01.mgmt: Scott Price is CEO; Jardine Matheson controls the company. The strategy has been portfolio simplification and cost discipline.
D01.comp: Watsons (AS Watson) in health and beauty, FairPrice and Sheng Siong in Singapore groceries, local convenience chains.
D01.moat: Store networks in dense Asian cities with prime locations, and scale in health and beauty buying.
D01.ind: Hong Kong retail is weak as residents shop in Shenzhen; Southeast Asian convenience retail is growing.
D01.risk: Hong Kong consumer spending continuing to leak to mainland China, which hits the most profitable Mannings business.
D01.implied: The price implies the turnaround holds and the divestments are complete.
D01.debate: Bulls say a restructured retailer with improving returns and a large dividend. Bears note Hong Kong structural weakness and years of underperformance.
D01.disprove: Hong Kong like-for-like sales declining; health and beauty margin compressing; Yonghui losses continuing; dividend cut.

S58.what: Provides airport ground handling, cargo handling and inflight catering at Changi and, after the WFS acquisition, at airports worldwide.
S58.rev: Gateway services (ground and cargo handling) is now the larger half after WFS; food solutions (inflight catering and central kitchens) the rest. Asia, Europe and the Americas.
S58.gm: Operating margins in the high single digits. Labour is the dominant cost; the business scales with flight and cargo volumes.
S58.mgmt: Kerry Mok is CEO. Temasek is a major shareholder. The WFS acquisition was large, debt-funded and initially controversial.
S58.comp: Swissport and Menzies in ground handling, dnata, and airline in-house handling units.
S58.moat: Airport concessions and long-term contracts with airlines, plus scale at Changi that is effectively a franchise position.
S58.ind: Air cargo volumes and passenger traffic are both growing; e-commerce air freight is a structural tailwind.
S58.risk: Air cargo volumes falling in a trade slowdown while the WFS debt remains, or a labour cost spiral.
S58.implied: The price implies continued deleveraging and margin improvement from the WFS integration.
S58.debate: Bulls say a global network now that the acquisition is integrating and debt is falling. Bears note the leverage and thin margins in a labour-intensive business.
S58.disprove: Net debt to EBITDA not falling; cargo volumes declining; labour costs rising faster than revenue; free cash flow not recovering.

M44U.what: Owns logistics warehouses across Singapore, Hong Kong, China, Japan, Australia, South Korea and Southeast Asia and leases them to logistics operators.
M44U.rev: Singapore roughly 25% of revenue, China ~20%, Hong Kong, Japan, Australia and Korea the rest. Over 180 properties.
M44U.gm: REIT metrics: net property income margin around 87% (logistics is cheap to run), gearing around 40%, occupancy above 95%.
M44U.mgmt: Managed by Mapletree Investments, a Temasek subsidiary with a large sponsor pipeline.
M44U.comp: ESR-REIT, Frasers Logistics and Commercial Trust, CapitaLand Ascendas in the same tenant pool.
M44U.moat: Geographic diversification and sponsor pipeline access. Individual warehouses are commodities; the portfolio scale is the advantage.
M44U.ind: Regional logistics demand is solid outside China; Chinese warehouse rents have been falling.
M44U.risk: China rental reversions staying negative while currency translation from the yen and renminbi reduces distributions.
M44U.implied: A distribution yield around 6-7% implies flat-to-declining distributions, which is what the market has recently seen.
M44U.debate: Bulls say a diversified logistics portfolio at a discount to book with a high yield. Bears point at China weakness, currency drag and rising borrowing costs.
M44U.disprove: China reversions still negative; portfolio occupancy below 95%; gearing above 41%; distribution per unit falling for a third year.

ME8U.what: Owns Singapore industrial properties - data centres, hi-tech buildings, business parks and flatted factories - plus US data centres.
ME8U.rev: Data centres are roughly 55% of assets under management and the strategic focus; hi-tech buildings, business parks and flatted factories the rest. Singapore ~50%, US ~45%.
ME8U.gm: REIT metrics: net property income margin around 74%, gearing around 40%, with data centre leases providing long weighted average lease expiry.
ME8U.mgmt: Managed by Mapletree Investments as sponsor - a Temasek subsidiary.
ME8U.comp: CapitaLand Ascendas REIT, Keppel DC REIT, Digital Realty and Equinix in data centres.
ME8U.moat: Data centre assets with power capacity that cannot easily be replicated in land-scarce Singapore - power allocation is the real scarcity.
ME8U.ind: Data centre demand is extremely strong; Singapore has had a moratorium on new capacity that favours existing owners.
ME8U.risk: US data centre tenant concentration and credit risk, plus higher refinancing costs on the US dollar debt.
ME8U.implied: A yield around 6% implies stable distributions with data centre growth offsetting flatted factory weakness.
ME8U.debate: Bulls say Singapore power-constrained data centres are a scarce asset. Bears note US tenant risk and rising interest expense.
ME8U.disprove: US data centre occupancy or tenant defaults; Singapore flatted factory reversions turning negative; gearing above 41%; distribution declining.

OV8.what: Runs a chain of about 80 value supermarkets across Singapore's heartland housing estates, plus a small China operation.
OV8.rev: Singapore supermarket retail is essentially all of revenue, with fresh produce a larger share of the basket than at competitors.
OV8.gm: Gross margin around 30-31% and steadily rising - unusual for a grocer - because of house brands, direct sourcing and a bulk-handling distribution centre.
OV8.mgmt: The Lim family founded and controls the business and runs it conservatively - net cash, no debt, consistent dividends.
OV8.comp: NTUC FairPrice (the dominant cooperative), Giant and Cold Storage (DFI), Prime and U Stars in the heartlands.
OV8.moat: Store locations in HDB estates won through competitive tenders, a low-cost operating model, and house brands that competitors cannot match on price.
OV8.ind: Singapore grocery is mature and grows with population and inflation; new HDB estate openings are the unit growth driver.
OV8.risk: Losing HDB store tenders to FairPrice or paying too much for them, or a slowdown in new store openings.
OV8.implied: A P/E in the 20s implies continued new store openings and gross margin expansion - it is priced as a quality compounder, not a cheap grocer.
OV8.debate: Bulls say a debt-free, family-run compounder with rising margins and a reliable dividend. Bears say the multiple is full for a grocer with a limited store runway in a small country.
OV8.disprove: Same-store sales declining; new store openings slowing; gross margin flattening; China operations losses widening.

V03.what: Designs and manufactures complex electronic products for global technology customers - life sciences instruments, networking, industrial and medical devices.
V03.rev: Life science and genomics, test and measurement, networking and communications, advanced industrial. Customer concentration is high and undisclosed by name.
V03.gm: Gross margin around 25-27%, high for contract manufacturing, because Venture does design work rather than pure assembly.
V03.mgmt: Wong Ngit Liong founded and chaired the company for decades; leadership transition is a live issue. Net cash balance sheet and a consistent dividend.
V03.comp: Flex, Jabil, Benchmark Electronics and Asian contract manufacturers.
V03.moat: Design-in relationships where Venture co-develops the product - switching manufacturer means re-qualifying the whole design.
V03.ind: Customer end markets (life sciences instruments, test equipment) have been in a prolonged destocking cycle.
V03.risk: Losing a major customer program, or the life sciences instrument market not recovering.
V03.implied: A mid-teens P/E with a large net cash position implies a modest recovery in customer demand.
V03.debate: Bulls say net cash, a high dividend yield and eventual customer recovery. Bears note revenue has declined for several years with no clear catalyst.
V03.disprove: Revenue declining again; gross margin below 25%; net cash being spent without returns; customer concentration disclosures worsening.

U06.what: Owns and develops Singapore commercial property - offices and malls in the CBD and suburbs - plus hotels, within the UOL and Wee family group.
U06.rev: Property investment (rental income) is the recurring core; property trading and hotel operations the rest. Almost entirely Singapore.
U06.gm: Look at rental income, occupancy at Singapore Land Tower and Marina Square, and the discount to net asset value.
U06.mgmt: Controlled by UOL Group and the Wee family. Conservative, low-leverage management with a long horizon.
U06.comp: CapitaLand, City Developments, GuocoLand and Frasers Property in Singapore commercial.
U06.moat: Prime CBD office assets - scarce, but this is asset ownership rather than a competitive advantage.
U06.ind: Singapore CBD office rents have been resilient with limited new supply.
U06.risk: An office demand downturn or the persistent net asset value discount never closing.
U06.implied: A deep discount to book implies the market gives little credit to the property valuations.
U06.debate: Bulls say quality Singapore offices at a large discount with a strong balance sheet. Bears say low free float and no catalyst mean the discount stays.
U06.disprove: Office occupancy falling; rental reversions negative; net asset value per share declining; no divestments or capital return.

8A8.what: Markets and distributes specialty prescription drugs in China, in-licensing products from overseas developers.
8A8.rev: Prescription drug sales in China across cardiovascular, gastroenterology, dermatology and ophthalmology. Note this is a Hong Kong-primary company with an SGX secondary listing.
8A8.gm: Gross margin is high (above 70%) as a pharmaceutical marketer, but Chinese volume-based procurement has compressed prices industry-wide.
8A8.mgmt: Founder Lam Kong is chairman with a controlling stake. Cash generation has been strong and dividends generous.
8A8.comp: Domestic Chinese pharmaceutical marketers and the multinational pharma companies whose products it licenses.
8A8.moat: A specialist salesforce covering Chinese hospitals and relationships with overseas licensors - a distribution position, not patents.
8A8.ind: Chinese pharmaceutical policy has been hostile to pricing through centralised procurement.
8A8.risk: Key products being added to volume-based procurement lists, which typically cuts prices by 50% or more.
8A8.implied: A single-digit P/E implies the market expects earnings to decline under Chinese pricing policy.
8A8.debate: Bulls say a cash-generative business with a high dividend at a very low multiple. Bears say Chinese drug pricing policy is a structural, not cyclical, headwind.
8A8.disprove: Core products entering procurement programmes; revenue declining; receivable days rising; dividend cut.

T14.what: Manufactures and sells traditional Chinese medicine, led by the Su Xiao Jiu Xin Wan cardiovascular pill, in China.
T14.rev: Traditional Chinese medicine manufacturing and distribution, with a small number of flagship products generating most of the profit. China only.
T14.gm: Gross margin around 40-45%. Proprietary formulations with brand recognition, but raw material (herb) costs are volatile.
T14.mgmt: State-linked ownership through Tianjin Pharmaceutical Group; a Chinese company with a primary SGX listing, which is unusual.
T14.comp: Tong Ren Tang, Yunnan Baiyao and other Chinese traditional medicine makers.
T14.moat: Protected traditional formulations, brand heritage and inclusion on provincial reimbursement lists.
T14.ind: Chinese traditional medicine has policy support but faces the same procurement price pressure as western drugs.
T14.risk: Raw herb cost inflation squeezing margins, or reimbursement list changes reducing volumes.
T14.implied: A low P/E and high dividend yield imply low growth expectations.
T14.debate: Bulls note strong cash generation and a generous dividend at a low multiple. Bears point at Chinese policy risk and limited disclosure for Singapore investors.
T14.disprove: Core product volumes declining; herb costs rising; reimbursement changes; related-party transactions with the state parent increasing.

J69U.what: Owns nine suburban shopping malls in Singapore - Causeway Point, Northpoint City, Waterway Point - located at MRT and bus interchanges.
J69U.rev: Suburban retail rent, almost entirely Singapore. Tenants are mostly necessity retail: supermarkets, food and beverage, services.
J69U.gm: REIT metrics: net property income margin around 72%, gearing in the high 30s, occupancy above 99%, rental reversions consistently positive.
J69U.mgmt: Managed by Frasers Property as sponsor, which provides an acquisition pipeline.
J69U.comp: CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust and Mapletree Pan Asia in Singapore retail.
J69U.moat: Malls physically integrated with MRT stations in dense residential catchments - the most defensible retail format in Singapore.
J69U.ind: Singapore suburban retail has been the strongest retail segment - necessity spending is resilient.
J69U.risk: Interest costs rising on refinancing, or acquisitions at yields below the cost of capital.
J69U.implied: A yield around 5% implies continued positive reversions and stable occupancy - it trades at a premium to most S-REITs for a reason.
J69U.debate: Bulls say the highest-quality suburban retail portfolio in Singapore with near-full occupancy. Bears say the premium valuation limits the return.
J69U.disprove: Rental reversions falling toward zero; occupancy below 98%; gearing above 40%; distribution per unit declining.
